terms.definition: A binding relationship established through promises and obligations. Biblical covenants describe God’s commitments and the response of His people.
The collection of books a religious community recognizes as Scripture; the biblical canon differs among Christian traditions.
A handwritten copy of a text, used as a witness when studying how biblical writings were transmitted.
The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, also called the Pentateuch; Torah can also mean instruction or law.
The departure of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, recounted in the biblical book of Exodus.
Forced removal from a homeland. In biblical history, it often refers to the deportation of Judeans to Babylon.
Anointed one. In Christian interpretation, Jesus is the promised Messiah; Jewish understandings of messianic expectation differ.
Good news. In Christianity, the message concerning Jesus Christ; a Gospel is also one of the four New Testament accounts of His life and ministry.
A story or comparison that invites listeners to consider a moral or spiritual teaching.
One sent with a commission. In the New Testament, a commissioned witness and messenger of Jesus Christ.
A learner or follower of a teacher; in the Gospels, someone who follows and learns from Jesus.
A person who speaks a message understood to come from God, often calling people to faithfulness and justice.
A message presented as coming from God. Biblical prophecy includes warning, encouragement, and promises, as well as predictions.
A sacred poem or song, especially one in the biblical Book of Psalms.
Biblical writings that explore wise living, human experience, suffering, and the fear of God, including Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes.
A letter. New Testament epistles address the beliefs and practices of early Christian communities and individuals.
A style of writing that uses visions, symbols, and heavenly revelation to address evil, judgment, and hope.
Being raised from the dead. Christianity centers its hope on the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The Christian belief that the eternal Son of God became human in Jesus Christ.
The restoration of a relationship damaged by sin; Christian traditions explain the saving work of Christ using several related models.
God’s freely given favor and help, received as a gift rather than earned.
Trust and reliance. In Christian teaching, a response of trust in God that shapes belief and conduct.
Turning away from sin and toward God, involving a change in understanding and action.
Release or rescue at a cost. Biblical writers use the image to describe deliverance from slavery, sin, or bondage.
Rescue or deliverance. In Christian teaching, God’s work of saving people from sin and restoring them to life with Him.
In Christian theology, being declared or made right with God; traditions differ in how they explain its relationship to faith, grace, and works.
The process or state of being set apart as holy, associated in Christian teaching with growth in a life shaped by God.
Being set apart for God; also the purity and distinctiveness attributed to God.
The portable sanctuary described in Exodus, associated with God’s presence among the Israelites during their wilderness journey.
The central sanctuary in Jerusalem where ancient Israelites offered worship and sacrifices.
A person set apart to serve in worship and sacred duties. Ancient Israelite priests served at the sanctuary and offered sacrifices.
An offering presented in worship, thanksgiving, dedication, or atonement.
The Jewish festival commemorating the Israelites’ deliverance from Egypt, especially the events described in Exodus 12.
The Greek name for the Jewish Feast of Weeks; in Acts 2, the occasion of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on Jesus’ followers.
The weekly day of rest and worship in Jewish tradition, rooted in the seventh day of the creation account.
A person who is not Jewish; a term often used in discussions of the early Church’s mission.
A member of a Jewish movement of the Second Temple period associated with careful observance and interpretation of Torah.
A person trained to copy, preserve, or interpret written texts; biblical scribes often worked with religious law.
A Christian rite using water, associated with initiation, cleansing, and identification with Christ; its form and interpretation vary among traditions.
The Christian meal of bread and wine recalling Jesus’ Last Supper, also called Communion or the Lord’s Supper; traditions differ in their explanation of Christ’s presence.
The Christian doctrine that the one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
God’s reign or rule, a central theme of Jesus’ teaching, expressed as both present activity and future fulfillment.
God’s bringing the world into being; in biblical studies, also the world understood as God’s handiwork.
The Christian term for humanity’s turning from God, traditionally associated with the disobedience in Genesis 3.
Thought, action, or a condition understood as contrary to God’s will and damaging to relationships with God and others.
The study of last things, including death, judgment, resurrection, and the ultimate fulfillment of God’s purposes.
Careful interpretation of a text using its words, literary form, and historical context.
The study of how texts are interpreted and how meaning is understood and applied.
A category of writing with shared conventions, such as narrative, poetry, law, letter, or apocalyptic vision.
An expression of grief, protest, or sorrow, often brought to God in prayer or poetry.
Worship of an idol or treating something other than God as the ultimate object of devotion.
A disclosure of what was previously hidden; in theology, God’s making Himself or His purposes known.
